extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media professionals, researchers, and general readers interested in the Steele dossier and journalistic publication ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and historical example about how journalists and institutions handled publication, briefing, and legal issues surrounding an unverified set of intelligence reports (the Steele dossier). Useful for deciding whether and how to publish or brief on raw intelligence or opposition research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify before publishing unconfirmed allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Many news organizations knew about the dossier but "chose not to publish information they could not confirm." CNN said it would not publish specific details because it had not "independently corroborated the specific allegations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat raw intelligence as a starting point for investigation and avoid publishing specifics unless independently corroborated. The New York Times described the dossier as "raw intelligence — not established facts, but a starting point for further investigation." Example: major outlets at Tabard Inn meetings promised Simpson they wouldn't write about the dossier itself, its author, or its path through government because they could not confirm it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly label raw intelligence and avoid presenting it as established fact
rubrics_metrics.description: The dossier was characterized as "raw intelligence — not established facts, but a starting point for further investigation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting material derived from raw intelligence, explicitly state its provisional status and avoid treating allegations as proven. Provide context that the material may contain rumor/hearsay and requires corroboration (Judge Karsnitz: "An intelligence report is simply a report of information potentially relevant to an investigation. It can take many forms, be true or false...").

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh public interest and circulation when deciding to publish
rubrics_metrics.description: BuzzFeed argued the materials were newsworthy because they were "in wide circulation at the highest levels of American government and media" and thus justified public release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether information circulating at high government/media levels makes it newsworthy despite lack of full verification. Courts have at times upheld publication on such grounds (judge in Superior Court of D.C. agreed with BuzzFeed's reasoning in dismissing a libel suit). Balance public's right to know against risks of harm and misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect sources and assess publication risk to source safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele and Fusion GPS expressed alarm that publication would endanger sources; Steele worried publication could have "compromised sources and methods" and put his source network at risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the danger to human sources and operations before publishing. Consider redactions, withholding identifying details, and whether disclosure could lead to retaliation or endanger lives (example: Glenn Simpson's plea to BuzzFeed to remove reports: "You are going to get people killed!").

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide sufficient context and controlled presentation rather than releasing raw documents wholesale
rubrics_metrics.description: Ben Smith later said he would still publish but "hold more tightly to the document... I wouldn't simply publish it as a PDF, destined to float free from our earnest caveats."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If publishing sensitive material, attach explanatory reporting, use curated excerpts or screenshots with context, and avoid dumping raw files that can be widely redistributed without context. This may limit misinterpretation and viral spread of unverified claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider editorial and ethical trade-offs of using anonymous or unverified sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication sparked debate about "the use of unsubstantiated information from anonymous sources." The Columbia Journalism Review initially backed BuzzFeed but later said the dossier "was never designed to meet the standards of good journalism."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize motivations and credibility of intermediaries and anonymous sources. Be transparent with readers about the provenance and limits of the sourcing and conduct internal postmortems when publication decisions have significant consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify and withhold sensitive material when briefings or disclosures would impinge on national security or ongoing investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: The FBI withheld parts of the dossier synopsis because material remained classified and "pertains to ongoing investigations or court proceedings, originated with a confidential source or describes confidential investigative techniques or procedures."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sharing with government officials or the public, withhold classified or investigative-sensitive content and follow legal/classification protocols. Use annexes/synopses that omit operational details to protect investigations and sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish legally between paid foreign-research expenditures and illicit foreign contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the legal difference between an "expenditure" by a campaign and a "contribution" to a campaign, hiring a foreign party to conduct research generally does not violate FEC laws forbidding foreign nationals from contributing to or aiding political campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing legality of opposition research or intelligence used in campaigns, evaluate whether the activity constitutes a campaign expenditure (permissible if properly declared) or a prohibited contribution/offer of aid (illegal). The Trump Tower meeting was contrasted as an illegal voluntary offer of aid, unlike Steele's contracted research.

rubrics_metrics.name: When serving as an intermediary, document chain-of-custody and be transparent about handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele delivered hard copies to intermediaries (e.g., McCain), and there were disputes about who provided the dossier to BuzzFeed; the founders of Fusion GPS defended using intermediaries to pass content to authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clear records of transfers and be transparent about who had access. Understand that intermediaries' decisions (e.g., whether to allow copying or photography) affect future publication and legal exposure; courts and later reporting scrutinized these custody decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure intelligence reports clearly with summary and detailed sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Each report started with a heading and was in two parts: a Summary section followed by a Detail section; summaries contained paragraphs based on numbered and expanded content in Detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing or evaluating intelligence-type reports, use a consistent heading/labeling format and separate concise summaries from detailed sourcing and evidence so consumers can rapidly assess claims and underlying material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and disclose uncertainties about source provenance and reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Inspector General's report stated Steele "was not the originating source of any of the factual information" and relied on a Primary Sub-source (Igor Danchenko) who used further sub-sources; the FBI noted concerns that the primary sub-source may not have been "completely truthful."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose limitations in the chain of sourcing, the degree of corroboration, and any known disputes about a source's truthfulness. Such transparency helps consumers evaluate the weight to give to allegations and prevents mischaracterization as settled fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating distinct legal/ethical issues when making public claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Public discussion conflated the dossier (contracted research) with the Trump Tower meeting (an alleged illegal offer of foreign assistance), but analysts emphasized they are legally different matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise in public claims and analysis: separate questions of legality, ethics, and probative value. Mischaracterizing the nature of an action (e.g., treating a contracted research expenditure as an illegal contribution) can mislead public understanding and legal analysis.
